ABOUT THE NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE
What are the dates for the NASA Space Apps Challenge?

The 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge will take place November 14-15, 2026.

What is the theme for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge?

Get ready to explore The Next Frontier! From your own backyard to the edges of the universe, discovery awaits at the NASA Space Apps Challenge. This is your opportunity to collaborate with a community of like-minded problem solvers to turn data into tools that benefit humanity and propel us to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Who should participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge?

The NASA Space Apps Challenge offers opportunities for students, technologists, and space science enthusiasts to better understand how to utilize NASA open data to respond to today’s most pressing science and space exploration challenges. No matter your age, skill level, or professional background, when you participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, you join a global community that embraces collaboration to develop projects and tools that improve life on Earth and in space.

Does it cost anything to participate?

There is no cost to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. If you are asked to pay money to participate in any aspect of a NASA Space Apps event, do not pay anything and please report to info@spaceappschallenge.org.

Can participants under the age of 18 participate? If so, how?

The NASA Space Apps Challenge is open to all ages! If under the age of 18, participants must be registered for the event by a parent or legal guardian and must be accompanied by a parent or legal guardian at all times during the event. Please note that Local Events may have additional requirements for persons under 18 to be eligible to participate in person. Check with your Local Lead for more information.

Additionally, participants under 18 should not:

Upload a photo of themselves as their Avatar or as part of their Team page
Use photo, video, voices, or likenesses of themselves or others under the age of 18 in their project demonstration or project submission.

Please carefully review the Participant Terms & Conditions as well as the Team Formation and Project Submission Guide for further guidance related to participants under 18.

Where does the NASA Space Apps Challenge take place?

The NASA Space Apps Challenge takes place at hundreds of events around the world. You may participate in an in-person or virtual Local Event near you or the virtual Universal Event if there is not an event near you.

Local Events are organized by Local Leads. Learn more about how to host a Local Event.

What should I do if I experience or witness discrimination, harassment, or any form of bullying during the hackathon or other NASA Space Apps activities?

We strive to ensure that NASA Space Apps is a place where all feel they belong, where all are comfortable being authentic, and where all are empowered to contribute to their fullest.

If you experience or witness discrimination, harassment, or any form of bullying during the NASA Space Apps Challenge, or have any other concerns, please contact your Local Lead and/or the NASA Space Apps Global Organizing (GO) Team at conduct@spaceappschallenge.org. The GO Team will take appropriate action, which may include warning or expelling offending participants from the event.

Where can I find the Participant Terms & Conditions?

The 2026 NASA Space Apps Participant Terms & Conditions can be found here.

NAVIGATING YOUR HACKATHON JOURNEY
How do I participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge?

To participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, you must:

Log in or create an account on our website.
Register for the NASA Space Apps Challenge starting on August 26, 2026.
Choose a Local Event near you or the virtual Universal Event.
Form or join a team to address one of the challenges. Team formation opens on September 17, 2026.
Join your Local Event on November 14-15, 2026. Look for their schedule and location details on the Local Event’s page.
Submit your project for judging according to the ending time of your Local Event.
How do I register?

Step 1: Access Your NASA Space Apps Account

Returning Participants: Log in to your existing NASA Space Apps account.

New Participants: Sign up for a NASA Space Apps account. Once you input your information, you will receive an email to verify your email address. You will verify your email by clicking the link in the message; afterwards you can log into the NASA Space Apps website.

Step 2: REGISTER FOR THE 2026 NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE & CHOOSE AN EVENT

Register: Registration for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge is open and will remain open through the end of the hackathon on November 15.

Complete the registration form on the 2026 Hackathon page, ensure that you complete all required questions and read the Terms & Conditions.

Choose a Local Event: We suggest that participants choose an in-person or virtual Local Event based on their physical location. The NASA Space Apps Challenge features hundreds of Local Events, allowing participants to find potential teammates located in the same community or time zone, or those who speak the same language.

Find a Local Event on the 2026 Local Events page. You can search by your location name or use the map to locate a Local Event near you. If there are no Local Events in your area, you can register for the virtual Universal Event.

If an event is at capacity, you can select to join the waitlist. If space becomes available, you will be added to the Local Event by the Local Lead. You can change your Local Event by clicking "Leave this Event" on the Local Event page you have chosen.

If there is not a Local Event near you, or you prefer to participate virtually, you can sign up for the Universal Event.

Step 3: Connect With Your Local Lead

Local Leads are the organizers of NASA Space Apps Challenge Local Events. They are available to answer questions and help connect you to potential teammates prior to the hackathon. Local Leads are the primary points of contact for your Local Event and will support your hackathon experience. You may find their contact information on your Local Event’s page. Please reach out to them as you prepare, and for specific details regarding your Local Event!

The NASA Space Apps GO Team will send updates about the hackathon with Space Apps Messages, you can check those from the menu under your profile icon. Additionally, your Local Lead may utilize Space Apps Messages to send updates about your Local Event.

Watch the Navigating the Hackathon: How to register video

What is the Universal Event?

The Universal Event is a virtual, asynchronous event that takes place November 14-15. Participants can create and join teams just like in Local Events, and registration works the same. Projects from the Universal Event are judged during the same overall judging period as all Local Event projects; however, Universal Event projects are evaluated only in comparison with other Universal Event submissions. The selection rate for Global Nominees is comparable across both the Universal Event and Local Events, reflecting an equally competitive nature.

However, we highly encourage participants to join a Local Event near them if they have the option rather than the Universal Event. Local Events provide access to a closer community, coaching opportunities, and many are in-person. You can find all available Local Events on the Local Events page, and you can change your Local Event at any time.

Universal Event Teams

You can form or join a team with anyone else registered for the Universal Event. For step-by-step instructions on how to join or form a team, check out the Team Formation Guide. In order to be eligible for global judging, a Universal Event Team must have at least two (2) participants. This rule only applies to the Universal Event.

Starting on November 3, use Space Apps Connect’s Find a Team category to connect with potential teammates. Space Apps Connect is the engagement platform where you can communicate with other participants, subject matter experts, local leads, global collaborators, and the Space Apps Global Organizing (GO) Team about everything related to Space Apps.

How do I learn more about each step of my hackathon journey? What are participant guides?

Throughout your hackathon journey, you will receive communications from the NASA Space Apps GO Team about updates and actions you need to take on spaceappschallenge.org as part of the hackathon. You will also receive information from your Local Lead about information specific to your Local Event.

Each year we provide Participant Guides to help you navigate each step of the hackathon. These provide step-by-step information to help you form teams, use Space Apps connect, submit your project, and learn about judging and awards. These guides can be found on the Resources page and will be updated prior to the hackathon:

September 17: Team Formation Guide
November 3: Space Apps Connect Guide
November 13: Project Submission Guide
November 13: Judging and Awards Guide

If you have a question not answered in the guides, reach out on our Contact Us page.

What are the challenges?

Challenges are authored by NASA and Space Agency Partner subject matter experts and encompass a wide variety of Earth and space science topics. Each team must select a challenge to address during the hackathon.

A summary of each challenge will be released on September 17, followed by challenge statements on October 28, which include the full details and requirements. Resources for each challenge will be published on November 13. Teams are not allowed to begin working on the challenges prior to the hackathon.

Do I need to be on a team? When can I join a team?

Yes, part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge experience is connecting with like-minded problem solvers from your own community and around the world! Participants are encouraged to create teams that include individuals with a variety of skill sets and backgrounds. Being on a team provides you with the opportunity to learn from one another and sets your team up for hackathon success.

Local Event teams must have at least one (1) person and Universal Event teams must have at least two (2) people to be eligible for global judging. Teams may have no more than six (6) members and must be signed up for the same Local Event or the Universal Event. You may only be on one team and teams are only permitted to work on one challenge. We highly recommend that you work with other participants.

Team formation for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge will open on September 17. Once team formation is open, you can join or create a team. Step-by-step instructions on how to create or join a team will be provided in the Team Formation Guide, which will become available on September 17.

Step-by-step instructions on how to create or join a team are provided in the Team Formation Guide.

How do teams submit their project?

In order to be eligible for Global Judging, teams must submit their project through their team’s project page on spaceappschallenge.org. Step-by-step instructions on how to submit your project will be provided in the Project Submission Guide, which will become available on November 13.

What is Super Intelligence? Can teams utilize it during the hackathon?

In accordance with the September 29, 2026 U.S. Executive Order, "the executive branch shall use the terms 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI.'"


Super Intelligence (SI) refers to computer systems that perform tasks typically associated with human reasoning, decision-making, content creation, and problem-solving. Examples include large language models, conversational assistants, image and video generation tools, foundation models, and code generation tools.


Participants may use SI tools to accelerate innovation, streamline development, and enhance creativity in support of their challenge solution. Each team's project submission must include a description of how SI tools were used during the development of their project.

What is Space Apps Connect?

Space Apps Connect serves as the collaborative communication forum for the NASA Space Apps Challenge community. It is completely FREE for registered participants to use. Joining Space Apps Connect is optional but highly encouraged. The platform allows you to connect with other hackathon participants as well as with Local Leads, Navigators, SMEs, Global Collaborators, and the NASA Space Apps Global Organizing (GO) Team. Space Apps Connect will open on November 3 and close at the conclusion of the hackathon.

Step-by-step instructions on how to navigate this platform will be provided in the Space Apps Connect Guide, which will become available on November 3.

Recognition and Awards

All NASA Space Apps Challenge participants will receive a certificate on their account’s profile page recognizing their participation upon submitting their project. Projects will then be judged on specific criteria to determine Honorable Mentions, Global Finalists, and Global Winners. Global Winners are announced upon the conclusion of judging. Global Winners will be invited to attend a virtual Winner’s Celebration in early 2027.

Learn more about this process in the Judging & Awards Guide.

NAVIGATING THE HACKATHON: PROJECT SUBMISSION
PROJECT SUBMISSION START & END TIMES

Project submission opens on Saturday, November 14 at 9:00 a.m. in accordance with the time zone of your team’s Local Event. At that time, your team will be able to edit your team’s Project page and submit your project. Project submission closes on Sunday, November 15 at 11:59 p.m. in accordance with the time zone of your team’s Local Event.

Exceptions: If your team is registered for the Universal Event, Project Submission opens Saturday, November 14 at 9:00 a.m. and closes Sunday, November 15 at 11:59 p.m. in accordance with the local time of your Team Owner's area of residence.

Check with your Local Lead about times for your Local Event’s local judging and awards which may differ from the global submission times.

EDITING YOUR PROJECT SUBMISSION PAGE

Once you create or join a team, you will be able to edit your team’s Project Submission page. The Project Submission page is where your team will provide all of the details about your project. This is the page that the judges will review. The more information you provide on this page, the better the judges can rate your submission!

How to Access Your Team’s Project Page

Click on your profile icon on the top right-hand side of the NASA Space Apps website menu.
Click on “My Team.”
On your team page, select the “Project” tab. Note: The “Project” tab will appear only when the hackathon begins on November 14, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. local time.

How to Edit Your Project Page

Click the blue “Edit” button.
Save your project often so you do not lose your work! You can save your work as many times as you like before the end of the hackathon by clicking the blue “Save Progress” button on the right-hand side of the page. Note that your changes will only be viewable to your team until you submit your project for judging.
To prevent multiple team members from editing the project page at the same time, toggle the edit "Lock" to 'ON'. This will let other team members know you are making changes to the "Project" tab. However, be aware that another team member can still remove the lock and make changes to the project, overwriting any changes you have not yet published. So, stay in close communication with your team members when editing.

Sharing Files to Your Project Submission Page

The Project page DOES allow for the upload or copy/paste of images (JPG, PNG, GIF up to 10MB). However, it DOES NOT allow for the upload of videos or documents.
Including Videos or Documents in Your Project Submission: Upload your files to a cloud service or repository (e.g., YouTube, Google Drive, GitHub, OneDrive, Dropbox, etc.) and share a publicly accessible link with no logins, permissions, or registrations required. If judges can’t access your project, it can’t be evaluated or judged.
Most platforms have a “share” option that provides a URL.
Before submitting:
Set the file to public access
Test the link in a private browser or with teammates to confirm it works.
You’re welcome to link to a slide deck, video, or other visual aids. For additional tools and resources, see the Global Collaborators page.
If you created a new website to host your project, we recommend requesting a Web Filter Classification to help ensure that judges can access your website. Please follow these steps:
Complete the FortiGuard Web Filter Classification form
.
Fill in required fields. Please note:
Category: You will need to select a category that best describes your site. This could include education, personal website and blogs, reference, or web-based application. NASA Space Apps is unable to make the categorization determination for you, so select the one from the choices in the form that best describes your final project.
Company Name: Write “N/A”
Submit your request for classification.

While this is not required for project submission, requesting a classification can help prevent potential website access issues during judging. Please note: the categorization of sites is ultimately at Fortiguard’s discretion and NASA Space Apps has no direct influence.

PROJECT PAGE FORM FIELD INSTRUCTIONS
Project Name

What is the name of your project?

High-Level Project Summary

Provide a high-level summary of your project. What did you develop? How does it address the challenge? Why is it important?

Link to Project Demo

Provide a short demonstration ("demo") of your project, either in the form of a 7-slide presentation (including title and introductory slides) or a 30-second or less video presentation. Upload your demo to an external site, a cloud-based hosting service, or code repository (e.g., YouTube, Google Drive, GitHub, One Drive, Dropbox, etc.) and provide a publicly accessible link. The link you provide should not require a password, permission, or registration in order to access your project demo. Review the "Tips for Creating a Project Demo" section for additional details.

This demo will be considered in your overall project evaluation, but the majority of judges’ evaluation will be based on your project submission. Note: a strong project demo can increase the potential for a high score in the Presentation category of the judging rubric.

Link to Final Project

Share a publicly accessible link to your final project. This can be a website you created to showcase your project, a cloud-based hosting service or code repository, or platforms such as YouTube, Google Drive, GitHub, One Drive, Dropbox, etc. The link you provide should not require a password, permission, or registration in order to access your final project. See “Sharing Files to your Project Submission Page” below for detailed instructions for sharing files.

Detailed Project Description

Provide additional details about your project. Some questions to consider are:

What exactly does it do?
How does it work?
What benefits does it have?
What do you hope to achieve?
What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Did you utilize any Super Intelligence (SI) tools and software in preparing your solution? If yes, how did you use them?

The use of SI tools, such as machine learning, chatbots, image generation, and large language models, is permitted for the NASA Space Apps Challenge and should be used as a tool to accelerate innovation and creativity for your challenge solution. SI should not be used to (come up with your idea of how to solve the challenge).

Generated content may not use, contain, or modify any NASA branding or design elements (such as the NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers). We require that you clearly indicate where and how SI tools were utilized in your project, including:

Images and videos: Must include a visible watermark to indicate SI generation .
Audio: Must acknowledge SI generation in descriptive text and metadata.
Code and data: Must acknowledge SI generation in descriptive text and metadata.

This SI question is for data‑collection purposes only, and your response will not be seen by the judges. However, judges will be able to see any SI‑generated indicators within your project—such as watermarks, descriptive text, or metadata. They will evaluate originality, intent, and execution based on the SI‑assisted elements you include and identify within your final project.

NASA Data

Provide specific details about what NASA data and resources you used. To be eligible for a Global Award, you must use at least one NASA data or resource.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

List all of the data, resources, and tools used in your project. Resources should include any code, text, and images (even if they are open source or freely available) that you used when creating your project. If you are using any copyrighted materials, make sure you have permission to use them.

You are also highly encouraged to use data or resources from the 2026 Space Apps Space Agency Partners. Many contributed to the resources found on each Challenge. This year’s Space Agency Partners are: Angola National Space Programme Management Office, Bahrain Space Agency, Brazilian Space Agency, CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation), Italian Space Agency, JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Center of the United Arab Emirates, National Space Activities Commission of Argentina, Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, Paraguayan Space Agency, Senegalese Space Studies Agency, Spanish Space Agency, Turkish Space Agency, and UK Space Agency.

TIPS FOR CREATING A PROJECT DEMO

Project Requirements

Demo: All teams must create a Project Demo as part of their project submission. The purpose of the demo is to provide the viewers and judges with a high-level summary of your project along with a demonstration of your final project, including any software or hardware that you created.
Format: Video (30 seconds or less) or slide deck (up to seven slides including title and intro slides).
Hosting: Use an external site (e.g., YouTube, Google Drive, GitHub, One Drive, Dropbox, etc.) for hosting your demo and ensure the link is publicly accessible. You will not be able to upload your video or slides to the NASA Space Apps website.
Language Requirements: You must use English language on the project submission page and in any linked materials. There is an exception: If your team chooses to create a video for the Project Demo, you can speak in another language, however, it MUST include English language subtitles. Slide decks must be in English.
Judging Criteria: Your project will be evaluated using five criteria: Impact, Creativity, Validity, Relevance, and Presentation. These categories are outlined in more detail in the 2026 Judging and Awards Guide.

Creating a Compelling Demo

Plan Ahead: Decide early whether to create a video or slide deck, and consider the question, “What story does my team want to tell?”
Delegate: Assign a teammate to lead the Demo creation.
Visual Storytelling: A great pitch can make all the difference in how your project is judged! Your goal should be to quickly communicate the importance and relevance of your project to someone who has no context, technical background, or previous knowledge of your subject. Regardless of your demo’s format, be sure to use strong visuals and ensure readability.
Video Demo: The video pitch must be 30 seconds or less.
[0:00] Introduce yourself: What is your name and your team's name?
[0:02] Lead us in: What challenge does your project address? What inspired you to choose this challenge?
[0:05] Name your project: Share your project's title and tagline to catch your audience's attention. Titles should be short but can indicate what problem the project solves or what people gain from your project.
[0:10] Describe your idea: How does it work? Display images or a prototype, describe a user's experience, and share how using NASA's free and open data and Space Agency Partner data made your proposed solution possible.
[0:20-0:30] Look into the future: Paint a picture! Captivate your audience with what it could be; What can your proposed solution do for people, the world, and beyond?
Slide Demo: The slide deck should be no more than seven slides (including the title and intro slides).
Choose a slide template with readable font size and limit the number of words on each slide when possible.
Incorporate strong visuals to help tell the story of your project. Your visuals should:
Display an image of the project
Describe the user experience
Include how NASA and space agency open and space based data and technology make your solution possible
Ensure that the content of your slides address the following:
Team name
Names of team members
The challenge your team selected
Limitations: Adhere to the 30-second and 7-slide limits. Projects that exceed these limits will not be eligible for Global Judging.

Past Global Winner Demo Examples

Get inspired by the exceptional demos from previous NASA Space Apps Challenge Winners. Click the "Project Tab" then scroll to the Demo section on each team’s Project page to see what makes a winning demo!

SUBMITTING YOUR PROJECT

In order for a project to be evaluated by our judges, teams must meet the following requirements:

All team members must be confirmed participants at the same Local Event in order for your team’s project to be eligible for awards. If you are waitlisted for a Local Event, please reach out to the Local Lead to request acceptance to the event. If the Local Lead declines or does not respond, each member of the team should switch to another Local Event that has room for all participants.
All required fields in the project form must be completed.
All content in the project form must be in English.
You must click the “Submit for Judging” button prior to Sunday, November 15 at 11:59 p.m. local time of your Local Event. If your team is registered for the Universal Event, you must click the “Submit for Judging” button prior to Sunday, November 15 at 11:59 p.m. in accordance with the local time of your Team Owner's area of residence. Any projects saved or submitted past this deadline will not be eligible for judging.
Project demonstrations and final projects may not include any images, video, audio, or other likeness to persons under 18 years old per the NASA Space Apps Terms & Conditions.

Once you’re ready to submit your project, follow these steps on the Project Submission page:

Check the box to agree to the "Terms and Conditions"
Check the box to agree to "Confirm All Work is Original"
Select “Submit for Judging.” If you have not completed all of the required sections on the Project page, you will not be able to submit.
If your project was submitted successfully, a banner will appear at the top of your screen along with a confirmation message. You may edit and resubmit your project as many times as you'd like until the end of the hackathon. Only your last saved submission will be reviewed by the judges.
ACCESSING YOUR PARTICIPANT CERTIFICATE

Participants who submit a project to the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge will receive a participant certificate. Certificates will automatically become available for download on your user Profile once your project is submitted. Please note that your team must click the “Submit for Judging” button prior to Sunday, November 15 at 11:59pm local time of your Local Event in order to earn a certificate.

To access your certificate:

Once logged in, click your profile icon and select “Profile” in the drop down.
Go to "Participant Information" and look for “2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.”
Click on the yellow “Download Participant Certificate” button to download. When downloading your certificate, make sure the selected paper size is “Letter” (8.5x11in / 215x297mm). Please note that the only downloadable format is a PDF version; we can not accommodate other versions.
We suggest downloading your participant certificate from a laptop or desktop, rather than a mobile device, to ensure proper formatting.
If you experience technical issues while downloading your participant certificate, please email web@spaceappschallenge.org and include your username and team name. As a reminder, certificates are only available for participants who submit a project.

Note that your name will appear on the certificate based on what you have listed under Full Name in your Profile. For your “Full Name," please provide your first and last name as you would like it to appear on your Participant Certificate. If you would like to modify your full name, you can do this by clicking on the “Change” button next to “Full Name” in the “Account Information” section in your Profile. You can change this at any time, even after submitting a project. In inputting your name, please adhere to the NASA Space Apps Values.

2026 NASA Space Apps Participant Terms and Conditions

Updated August 7, 2026

BY PARTICIPATING IN THE NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE, THE PARTICIPANT (YOU) AGREES TO THE FOLLOWING TERMS AND CONDITIONS:

"Participant" or "you" means an individual who registers for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

"NASA" or "Agency," as used herein, means the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and includes its support contractors (at any tier) that are assisting NASA with the planning and execution of the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

PARTICIPATION
Participation in the NASA Space Apps Challenge (or "Space Apps," or "the event") or the Winners Celebration (a virtual award ceremony for Global Winners) is fully voluntary, and participants are not entitled to compensation, nor will they be considered employees, agents, independent contractors, or consultants of NASA or of the United States (U.S.) Federal Government. Individuals who participate in the event shall engage in their personal capacity only, including identifying themselves by their own names. If a Participant works for a U.S. Federal Government support contractor, that individual shall not reference the fact that they are a U.S. Federal Government support contractor, nor shall any work performed for or in support of the event be performed pursuant to or charged under such contract. All U.S. Federal Government contractor employee participation shall be done on a voluntary basis outside of the participant’s working hours, and these participants shall not receive or be entitled to any compensation for the time that they spend preparing for or participating in the event. U.S. Federal Government civil servant employees are not eligible to register as Participants.

The NASA Space Apps Challenge will be held at each NASA Space Apps Challenge location starting on November 14, 2026 (or a different day during the same week previously expressly approved in writing by the NASA Space Apps Global Organizing Team). Prior to the start time, you must be registered to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge online at https://spaceappschallenge.org (a list of locations will be provided in August 2026). Participants who are under the age of 18 are required to be registered for the event by a parent or legal guardian and must be accompanied during the event at all times by a parent or legal guardian. By signing up for an account and/or registering for an event, you permit the NASA Space Apps Challenge to send information about the event and future events, as well as notification messages, to your registered email address.

NASA welcomes broad participation in NASA Space Apps. Please note that NASA policy limits NASA’s ability to participate, collaborate, or coordinate with China, including Hong Kong and Macau. Participation is based on affiliation with a China or a Chinese-owned entities, including universities, not based on Chinese nationality. Space Apps participants may not participate in Space Apps in connection with an affiliation with China or a Chinese-owned entity, and participants may not participate, collaborate, or coordinate with China or any Chinese-owned entity in relation to their participation in the NASA International Space Apps Challenge.

SUBMISSIONS:
All submitted solutions ("Solutions") shall directly address one or more of the NASA Space Apps Challenge statements ("Challenges") as described at https://spaceappschallenge.org/ to be eligible for posting on the NASA Space Apps website. Solutions that do not address a specific Challenge may be posted publicly at NASA’s sole discretion. By submitting a Solution, you grant NASA permission to display, copy, combine, compile, distribute, and disseminate your Solution to support the NASA Space Apps Challenge. All Solutions will be posted at NASA's sole discretion. Solutions will not be accepted or posted if they include:

Threatening, slanderous, or obscene language;
Personal attacks;
Discriminatory language (including hate speech) based on race, national origin, age, gender, sexual orientation, religion, or disability;
Sexually explicit material or other material that would violate the law;
Material that promotes commercial services or products;
Proprietary or business sensitive information that you do not have the right to make public;

THE PURPOSE OF NASA SPACE APPS

While awards are an exciting and compelling reason to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, remember that, at its core, NASA Space Apps is a collaborative event—not a competitive one. We hope that participants have the opportunity to learn, grow, and share. We celebrate all of your ideas and efforts, whether you receive an award or not.

All participants that submit a project on the website by the deadline will receive a certificate of participation.

NAVIGATING THE HACKATHON: JUDGING & AWARDS
ELIGIBILITY FOR GLOBAL JUDGING

To be eligible to advance to Global Judging from either a Local Event or the Universal Event, your team and project must meet certain requirements. See the Project Submission Guide for step-by-step details on how to submit your project.

Minimum requirements:

Respond to one of the official NASA Space Apps Challenges.
Ensure that all team members are registered for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, have chosen the same Local Event (and are not waitlisted) or Universal Event, and appear on the Members tab of your Team’s page. Teams will not be able to add new members after project submission has closed. Local Event teams must have at least one (1) person and Universal Event teams must have at least two (2) people to be eligible for global judging. Teams may have no more than six (6) members. Note: All teammates, including the Team Owner, must be registered for the same Local Event. Teams that do not meet this requirement are not eligible for Global Judging.
Complete all of the required fields on the Project Submission page.
Provide a short demonstration ("demo") of your project, either in the form of a slide presentation (7-slide limit including title and intro slides) or a video presentation (30-second limit).
Use English language on the project submission page and in any linked materials. Exception: If your team creates a video for your Project Demo, you can speak in another language. However, it MUST include English language subtitles.
Submit your project by navigating to the Project tab on your team page, click edit, and then "submit" before Sunday, November 15 at 11:59 p.m. local time in accordance with your team’s Local Event. Exception: If your team is registered for the Universal Event, your project must be submitted in accordance with the local time of the Team Owner. Contact your Local Lead if you have questions about the deadline for your Local Event.
Agree to and check the box on the project submission page that says: "I have read and understand the project submission requirements as contained in the NASA Space Apps Project Submission Guide, and I agree to the Participant Terms and Conditions and Privacy Policy."
Agree to and check the box on the project submission page that says: "I confirm that the submitted project represents my team’s original work and that all external resources including code, text and images (even if they are open source or freely available) used in the project are listed in the References field of the project submission form. In creating our solution, my team has not used any copyrighted materials (i.e., music, images, text, etc.) that we don’t have permission to use."
In accordance with NASA’s China funding restriction policy, teams will undergo review for prohibited bilateral activity with China, or a Chinese-owned entity, in order to be determined eligible to participate in the Global Judging round of NASA Space Apps. China or Chinese-owned entity” means any department, agency, or instrumentality of the government of China and any governmental subdivision thereof, including Hong Kong and Macau, any company owned by China, or any company, university, or similar institution incorporated under the laws of China or any governmental subdivision thereof, including Hong Kong and Macau. Any determination of eligibility shall be made by NASA, in its sole discretion, and will be based on information provided by the applicant. Please refer to the NASA Space Apps Terms and Conditions for Chinese affiliation’s impact on eligibility to be recognized as a NASA Space Apps Global Winner.
JUDGING CRITERIA

At every level of judging, from Local and Universal Events to Executive Judging, your project will be evaluated on a scale of 1-to-5, in each of the following criteria:

Impact

This project makes an impact by addressing either a minor or major problem, which influences the quality and quantity of its overall effect. The extent to which it inspires or helps others varies, ranging from a broad audience to a select few.

Score of 5 (Outstanding Impact): This project demonstrates exceptional impact, addressing a significant problem with proposed solutions. Its reach is extensive, inspiring, benefits a large audience, or could change the world. The quality and effectiveness of the project far exceeds expectations, setting a high standard for others.

Creativity

This project demonstrates originality and innovation. It introduces a novel concept that has not been attempted before or presents an improvement upon existing ideas in a meaningful way. This project is distinguished by its level of creativity, showcasing a fresh perspective or inventive execution.

Score of 5 (Highly Creative and Innovative): This project showcases remarkable creativity, introducing a groundbreaking approach that has never been attempted before. It challenges conventional methods, presenting an original and inventive proposed solution that stands out in its field. The uniqueness of the idea makes it a true innovation.

Validity

This project presents a proposed solution that is grounded in scientific principles and demonstrates technical, functional, or logical feasibility. It is designed to effectively achieve its intended purpose and has the potential to function in real-world applications. The completeness of the proposed solution varies—it may be fully developed or still require significant refinement. Additionally, the usability and user-friendliness of the project influence its practicality and accessibility.

Score of 5 (Highly Valid and Feasible): This proposed solution is scientifically sound and technically feasible, demonstrating strong alignment with established principles. It is fully developed and ready for real-world implementation, effectively achieving its intended purpose. The project is highly usable and user-friendly, making it accessible and practical for widespread application.

Relevance

This project fully and directly addresses the challenge for which it was submitted, demonstrating a strong alignment with the intended objectives. It meaningfully integrates NASA data, utilizing it as a core component of the proposed solution rather than a superficial addition. The depth of engagement with the data enhances the project's credibility and effectiveness.

Score of 5 (Highly Relevant and Strong NASA Data Integration): This project thoroughly engages with the challenge, delivering a proposed solution that is deeply connected to the intended goals. NASA data is integral to the project’s success, providing meaningful insights that drive the innovation forward. The use of data is well-executed, enhancing both the credibility and impact of the solution.

Presentation

The team effectively communicated their project, clearly conveying the challenge, their proposed solution, and its significance. The storytelling was engaging and well-structured, ensuring the audience understood the project's purpose and impact. The clarity, organization, and delivery of their presentation played a key role in making their ideas compelling and clear. Judges evaluate the demo and full project to compute this score.

Score of 5 (Exceptional Communication and Storytelling): The team delivered a well-structured and compelling presentation, clearly articulating the challenge, proposed solution, and importance of the project. Their storytelling was engaging, allowing the audience to fully grasp the significance and potential impact of the work. The delivery was polished, structured, and highly effective in communicating their ideas.

While many NASA Space Apps Challenge teams consider the first four judging criteria carefully and excel at developing projects with great potential, remember to pay equal attention to the final criterion: presentation. We recommend devoting time and resources to developing your pitch and building a great story around your project. Be sure to recruit team members with a variety of skills, including expertise in areas like storytelling and design, to help document your project and share the value of your proposed solution with the world. For tips on how to craft an effective project demo, read the Project Submission Guide.

PHASE 1: LOCAL EVENT JUDGING & GLOBAL NOMINEES

Following the hackathon, Local Event and Universal Event judges will determine the projects that will advance to Global Judging. These selected teams are known as Global Nominees.

Global Nominees from both Local Events and the Universal Event will be announced on December 3, 2026.

Local Event Judging & Global Nominee Selection

Following the hackathon, all project submissions from each Local Event will be evaluated by a panel of Local Judges, who are recruited, trained, and organized by the designated Local Lead. Using the NASA Space Apps judging criteria, the panel will select projects to advance to Global Judging.

Local Leads and Local Judges have the option to provide local awards. These local awards are separate from the Global Judging process and Global Winners that will be announced after all phases of judging are complete. Regardless of Local Judging results, only officially submitted Global Nominees will be considered for Global Judging.

Universal Event Judging Process

Following the hackathon, all projects submitted to the Universal Event will be evaluated by a team of subject matter experts (SMEs). Using the NASA Space Apps judging criteria, the Universal Event Judges will select projects to advance to Global Judging. These teams will be known as “Global Nominees.” The number of Universal Event teams that will advance to Global Judging will be proportional to the number of projects that advance to Global Judging from Local Events.

PHASE 2: GLOBAL FINALISTS & HONORABLE MENTIONS

During Global Judging, all Global Nominees will be reviewed by a team of expert judges. Each project will be evaluated according to the judging criteria in this guide. These votes will determine the top teams, who will be known as the “Global Finalists.”

Global Finalists will be announced on December 17, 2026. We also recognize Honorable Mentions at this time. While not advancing to Executive Judging or eligible for awards, Honorable Mentions were ranked highly by our Global Judges for their ingenuity and creativity.

PHASE 3: GLOBAL WINNERS

The Global Finalists will be reviewed by an executive committee from NASA and the 2026 Space Agency Partners. These judges are agency leaders and executives with a variety of subject matter expertise. Each Global Finalist project will be evaluated by each executive judge. This committee will nominate teams for one of ten Global Awards:

Best Use of Science: The project that makes the best and most valid use of the scientific method.
Best Use of Data: The project that best makes space data accessible or leverages it to a unique application.
Best Use of Technology: The project that exemplifies the most innovative use of technology.
Galactic Impact: The project with the most potential to improve life on Earth or the universe.
Best Mission Concept: The project with the most plausible concept and design.
Most Inspirational: The project that captures our hearts.
Best Storytelling Award: The project that most creatively communicates the potential of open data through the art of storytelling.
Global Connection Award: The project that best connects people around the world through technology.
Art & Technology Award: The project that most effectively combines technical and creative skills.
Local Impact Award: The project that demonstrates the greatest potential for making a difference in their local community.

The team or individual that creates the winning submission for each of the categories above will be known as the “Global Winners” and will be announced on January 26, 2027. Global Winners will also be invited to attend a virtual Winner’s Celebration in early 2027.

Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
Join the Challenge
DetailsResourcesTeams
Event
2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge
Difficulty
Advanced
Intermediate
Subjects
Earth Science
Software

Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response. Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots, enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

BACKGROUND

Fire regimes

Some ecosystems need periodic fires to maintain their function and their structure. However, changes in fire intensity, extent, and frequency can have negative impacts on climate, society, and biodiversity, along with the ecosystem services they provide. Fires can also cause loss of life and properties, degradation of health, and acute risk to fire managers.

Because humans have modified global patterns of vegetation, ignition, and climate over millennia, fires on both local and global scales are increasingly human-related.

Burning activity involves wildfires in natural vegetation and forested areas, as well as anthropogenic fires associated with agriculture, land-clearing, waste disposal, and industrial activities. It is one of the many dynamic phenomena that can be detected with remote sensing.

Satellite fire detection and monitoring

Climate models project that fire weather will become more common and more intense. Earth Observation (EO) satellites provide technological solutions for early detection, rapid response, and postfire assessment, measuring thermal radiation and smoke across regional to global scales.

Detecting hotspots on Earth's surface

EO satellites provide information on fire location, intensity, and temporal evolution. Satellite sensors operating in the thermal infrared (TIR) range can detect hotspots on the Earth's surface generated by urban and wildfires, volcanic eruptions, and industrial processes such as gas flares in oil and gas operations.

For active fires, detection and monitoring rely mainly on mid-infrared (MIR) and TIR measurements, where active combustion produces its stronger signal. Sensors such as MODIS and VIIRS provide real-time thermal anomaly detection, enabling early hotspot identification and the assessment of burned areas.

Burn activity calendars

Using satellite-detected hotspots, fire activity calendars can be developed by integrating historical information with recent data, allowing for the rapid visual identification of seasonal patterns, anomalies, and trends in each region.

MODIS sensors on board Terra and Aqua satellites provide more than two decades of observations, but they are approaching the end of their operational life and are being replaced by VIIRS sensors. Their records cannot be directly compared without harmonization, since MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions, sensitivities, and observation schedules.

Therein lies the root of the challenge. As fire frequency and intensity increase, emergency managers benefit from an updated and consistent hotspot calendar that enables them to rapidly visualize, for example, which month and years had the highest fire activity, and compare the burning activity of the current month against the historical median for a selected area.

You may consider harmonizing NASA Earthdata FIRMS hotspots, combining the extensive historical series of MODIS with the continuity and greater detail of VIIRS.

Emergency managers could then use the web application to monitor sensitive regions, recognize changes relative to historical patterns, and strengthen fire forecasting and response.

OBJECTIVES

Your challenge is to develop a harmonized burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots in a web application, combining the extensive historical series of MODIS with the continuity and greater detail of VIIRS to provide a consistent time series of hotspot activity.

This challenge could be approached in two parts. The first is MODIS and VIIRS hotspot harmonization, so that by the end of that phase the sensor of origin no longer matters and the patterns, trends, and anomalies become the focus.

The second involves developing a web application that takes harmonized hotspot data as input. Through this visual tool, a user could select a region and a specific date range, then download analytics and visualizations of fire activity.

A calendar of burning activity showing the number of hotspots detected from the early 2000s to the present, built on the harmonized hotspots dataset and integrated into the web application, would give emergency managers a view of the fire history of an area: which periods of the year see more fires, which years had more burning activity, and how a current fire compares with previous ones.

In addition to numerical information, you could consider how color ramps might represent similarities and differences in the number of detected hotspots across months, providing an accessible and intuitive way to visualize fire activity. A downloadable CSV File of hot spots detected during a search would be another useful output.

POTENTIAL CONSIDERATIONS

You may (but are not required to) consider the following:

Your target audience can include early warning and emergency responders, scientists, land managers, and firefighters.
Consider making your web application interactive – for example, a map where users can draw the area of interest, or an option to enter latitude and longitude.
Consider using accessible color ramps.
Your tool could depict a burning calendar
Your tool could focus on a few key indices and figures and present them through data visualizations, such as:
Historical comparisons, including anomalies against multi-year averages
Number of fires detected and reported

For data and resources related to this challenge, refer to the Resources tab at the top of the page. More resources may be added before the hackathon begins.
